To diagnose means to carefully examine something — a person, a machine, a system, or even a situation — and then identify what is wrong with it and why. It is not just noticing that something is wrong. It is figuring out the specific nature of the problem after a thoughtful, evidence-based process.

Think of it this way: if your car makes a strange noise, you know something is wrong. But a mechanic diagnoses the problem — meaning, after examining it, they tell you: "This is a worn-out timing belt." That act of moving from "something is wrong" to "here is specifically what is wrong, and here is why" — that is diagnosing.

Diagnosing always involves a process. It is never a random guess. It generally follows three steps:

1. Observe the signs or symptoms. Something appears to be wrong. There are clues — unusual behaviour, pain, errors, or failure.

2. Examine and analyse. The person diagnosing gathers information, asks questions, runs tests, and studies the evidence carefully.

3. Reach a conclusion. Based on everything gathered, a specific problem is identified. This conclusion is the diagnosis (the noun form — the result of diagnosing).

So when you diagnose something, you are doing all three of these things together.

Although "diagnose" is most commonly associated with medicine, it is used in many areas of life:

In medicine — the most classic use. Doctors, dentists, and vets diagnose illnesses and conditions.

A doctor diagnoses a patient with high blood pressure after checking their readings and reviewing their symptoms.

In technology and computing — engineers and IT professionals diagnose faults in hardware or software.

A technician diagnoses the issue with the laptop as a corrupted operating system.

In mechanics and engineering — to identify what is wrong with a machine or structure.

The engineer diagnosed a crack in the bridge's foundation as the cause of the instability.

In everyday problem-solving — you can use it more generally whenever someone carefully identifies the root cause of any problem.

The manager diagnosed the team's low productivity as a result of unclear goals.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"Diagnose" follows a few common and reliable patterns:

Pattern 1: diagnose + someone + with + condition
This is the most common pattern. The person or thing with the problem comes first, then "with," then the name of the problem.

The doctor diagnosed her with asthma.
The vet diagnosed the dog with an ear infection.

Pattern 2: be diagnosed with + condition (passive)
This is when the focus is on the person receiving the diagnosis, not on who did the diagnosing.

He was diagnosed with diabetes last year.
She was diagnosed with anxiety at the age of 25.

Pattern 3: diagnose + the problem + as + something
Used when describing what the specific fault is, rather than diagnosing a person.

The mechanic diagnosed the fault as a leaking radiator hose.
The specialist diagnosed the issue as a vitamin D deficiency.

Pattern 4: diagnose + the condition directly
Sometimes the object of the verb is just the condition itself, without naming the person.

The physician diagnosed pneumonia from the X-ray.
The engineer diagnosed a software conflict.

Anyone who has the knowledge and information to carefully examine a problem and identify its cause can diagnose. It does not always require a doctor or a formal expert — though in serious situations (especially medical ones), an expert is needed and expected.

  • A doctor diagnoses a disease.
  • A mechanic diagnoses a car fault.
  • A plumber diagnoses a pipe blockage.
  • A teacher diagnoses a student's learning difficulty.
  • You can even diagnose your own problem — this is called self-diagnosing, though it carries risks if done without proper knowledge.

The key is that diagnosing requires careful thinking and evidence. It is not a casual guess.

It helps to understand the boundaries of the word:

  • It is not the same as treating or fixing. Diagnosing only identifies the problem. What comes after — the cure, the repair, the solution — is separate. You diagnose first, then you treat.
  • It is not the same as detecting. To detect something simply means to notice or find it. To diagnose goes further — you must identify what the problem actually is and why it is happening. A smoke alarm detects smoke; a firefighter diagnoses what caused the fire.
  • It is not guessing. A diagnosis is based on evidence. If someone jumps to a conclusion without proper examination, that would not truly be a diagnosis — that would be an assumption.

Since you will encounter these forms often, here they are:

  • Diagnose — the verb (what you do): "The doctor will diagnose the condition."
  • Diagnosed — past tense: "She was diagnosed last Monday."
  • Diagnosing — present participle: "The team is diagnosing the system error."
  • Diagnosis — the noun (the result): "The diagnosis was diabetes."
  • Diagnoses — plural noun: "He received two separate diagnoses."
  • Diagnostic — the adjective (relating to diagnosing): "They ran a diagnostic test."
  • Diagnostics — noun referring to tools or tests used to diagnose: "The computer ran a full diagnostics check."

To diagnose is to move from uncertainty to clarity — to examine something carefully, piece together the evidence, and name the specific problem. It is deliberate, evidence-based, and always comes before any attempt at a solution. While it is most associated with medicine, it applies to any situation where someone must identify the root cause of a problem through careful examination and reasoning.
